articles.title: Find out what’s filling your database
articles.dek: Core and Container installations receive the Storage page too, with measurements taken on request.
body: Sort the new Storage report by size to find which sensor is keeping the most history, then open its settings directly from the list. Home Assistant’s Database card separates recorded states from statistics and lets administrators search for individual items.
A breakdown by table shows how the different parts of the history store contribute to the total. Per-item sizes are estimates; some database configurations can report row counts without byte sizes.
The Refresh button takes a new measurement when requested. Core and Container installations need the recorder, Home Assistant’s history component, enabled to show the card.

Add database usage card to the storage page
Document the database card on the storage page

media.alt: Home Assistant Storage page with a Database card showing table sizes and a list of entity storage estimates.

articles.title: Set your blinds by dragging their picture
articles.dek: The panel keeps the reported position separate from the requested one, so a command does not look like completed movement.
body: Labeled Open, Stop and Close buttons sit beside an interactive drawing in Home Assistant’s redesigned shutter, blind and garage-door panel. A tap or drag chooses a position; equipment without position control uses an open-or-close gesture instead.

The picture follows what the device reports, with a separate marker for its target. Keyboard and screen-reader controls remain available, and a switch selects tilt adjustment where the device supports it.

pullRequests.title: Redesign the cover more-info dialog

media.alt: Redesigned Home Assistant shutter controls with a shutter drawing and labeled Open, Stop and Close buttons.

articles.title: See which walls stand between connected devices
articles.dek: Separate maps accommodate several floors or buildings, with battery levels and failed connections as optional layers.
body: A weak connection means more when its route crosses the rooms you know. Uploading a floorplan to Z-Wave JS UI lets owners place their devices on it and trace the path back to the controller.

Current and backup routes, neighboring devices and network-health indicators can be shown together or hidden individually. Clicking a device opens its usual details, and maps are included in backups by default.

Steve Berg tested the view on a network of about thirty-seven devices. Owners position the devices themselves, and route information builds as they communicate, so a map can initially lack routes after a restart.

pullRequests.title: feat(ui): floorplan mode for the network graph

media.alt: Z-Wave JS UI floorplan with device nodes, route lines and battery indicators.

articles.title: Talk through a camera over a local HTTP connection
articles.dek: The Android app requests microphone permission and stops sending audio when the page closes or the app moves into the background.
body: An unencrypted connection to Home Assistant can prevent the browser from supplying microphone audio. The Android companion app provides a native audio path in that situation, allowing two-way conversations through compatible cameras.
The camera still needs to support two-way audio; the app does not add that capability to equipment that lacks it.

pullRequests.title: Add support for 2way audio in frontend
Document two-way audio for cameras

articles.title: A simpler way to find the right community project
articles.dek: A Marketplace proposal would explain the next step after installation; curation and mobile designs remain open questions.
body: Looking for a way to track energy or add devices could become a starting point for discovery. Laura is shaping a Home Assistant Marketplace page organized both by those goals and by types such as dashboard cards, integrations and themes.

A proposed detail page puts a plain-language summary and practical instructions above the developer’s project notes. It would explain where a card or theme appears, keep updates visible on the Installed page, and identify the project as community-made and not tested or reviewed by Home Assistant.

The approach uses existing catalog information apart from a small curated set of goal-based lists. Who maintains those lists, how they fit with integration categories, and the mobile and dark-mode designs remain unresolved. Changing the installation process is outside this proposal.

articles.title: A new sign-in route restores ARD Sounds accounts
articles.dek: Existing password-based setups need to be linked again; radio, search and public podcasts continue without authentication.
body: A code confirmed on ARD’s own website replaces the password entry that stopped working in Music Assistant. ARD had restricted password login to its captcha-protected page and moved subscription data away from the service the integration used.

Subscribed podcasts synchronize with the Music Assistant library, and listening progress travels in both directions, with the newer position taking precedence. Adding or removing an ARD podcast also changes the subscription in the ARD account.

Music Assistant no longer stores the ARD password, and an account-service outage preserves the existing subscription list. Peter Meiser tested sign-in, subscriptions, listening progress and session renewal with a real account.

pullRequests.title: Fix ARD Sounds account login and sync subscriptions and progress

articles.title: A clearer place in a long audiobook
articles.dek: Podcasts receive the same treatment, with tabs separating chapters from bookmarks on detail pages.
body: Instead of overlapping labels, the listening timeline in Music Assistant has a segment for each chapter and a ‘Chapter X of Y’ indicator between the timestamps. The fullscreen player leads with the current chapter’s title, keeping the book or episode and its author underneath.

The queue lists chapters and bookmarks with their start times and keeps the current chapter in view. Tapping the chapter count switches between progress through that section and progress through the whole book or episode.

body: Power, operating mode, target temperature and fan speed become Home Assistant controls through a wired serial connection. The first version supports the Intesis INMBSMHI001R000, a gateway serving a single air-conditioning unit.
Where the unit has a movable vane, its swing position can be controlled too. Other gateway models are outside this initial support.

articles.title: Plan charging around the cheapest electricity
articles.dek: Zonneplan’s hourly and quarter-hourly contracts are covered, using data already fetched for the account.
body: Finding an inexpensive overnight block takes more than the current rate or the next one. A new Home Assistant action returns the full available Zonneplan price schedule, so an automation can compare intervals before choosing when to charge.
Each entry includes its start, end and all-in price per kilowatt-hour. Calling the action makes no additional request to Zonneplan.

body: Blank placeholders in Home Assistant’s media browser give way to a frame chosen near the event that triggered the recording. Cards using the same media source can display it too.

The browser also cancels image requests that are no longer needed, preventing an entire page of previews from holding up playback. Michał Jonik makes a first contribution to Home Assistant Core with the recording previews.

articles.title: Add DLNA speakers that don’t show up automatically
articles.dek: An advanced setting accepts a device address or description URL; the first route depends on how the equipment responds.
body: A receiver on a separate part of the home network can be missed during Music Assistant’s usual search. For equipment using DLNA, a standard for sharing media over a network, owners can supply its numeric IPv4 network address or the HTTP or HTTPS address of its device-description document.

The numeric address triggers a targeted search; the document connects directly. Offline manual devices are retried every minute. Mark tested the document route with a Denon receiver on a separate network segment, making a first contribution to Music Assistant’s server. That receiver did not answer the targeted search.

Martijn van der Pol adds ways to set a shutter or blind by name in a room or on a floor, or to address a whole type, such as blinds, on a floor. Lights and fans can likewise be switched off across a floor.

articles.title: Backup Wi-Fi takes over when a hidden network is missing
articles.dek: ESP8266 devices were unaffected; the failing connection sequence dates back to the 2025.11 release.
body: A device could get stuck retrying connections after its preferred hidden network proved out of range. A delayed failure notification then disrupted each subsequent attempt, preventing ESPHome from joining another saved network.
On an ESP32-PICO-D4 test setup, the correction connected after all four resets, while the affected build failed to connect during the comparison runs.

articles.title: A safeguard for identity and keys during controller restores
articles.dek: Protection extends to older firmware, but cannot help when the backup’s final byte contains data.
body: Losing manufacturing information during a Z-Wave backup restore can change a controller’s security identity and prevent signed firmware updates. The hazard affects Home Assistant Connect ZWA-2: writing the end of a backup can erase a neighboring part of memory.

Z-Wave JS avoids that boundary when the backup ends in unused space. Otherwise, the restore proceeds with a warning. The author has verified the safeguard with automated tests, but has not tested it on hardware.

pullRequests.title: fix: work around NVM restore erasing the flash page after the NVM

articles.title: Readings recover after a device restart
articles.dek: Low-power sleep keeps its existing shutdown order so an expected pause remains distinct from a lost connection.
body: An unchanged sensor value could leave Home Assistant showing ‘unavailable’ even after an ESPHome device reconnected. A message sent too late during shutdown made the next identical reading look like a duplicate.

Devices without deep sleep—the low-power mode that temporarily suspends operation—send the queued readings their connection can accept before announcing the disconnect. That ordering prevents stale readings from hiding the device’s return after a restart or firmware update.
